Chapter 11 — Decision Trees and Ensembles

Every model of the previous chapters computes one number from the features by a single formula that is the same everywhere in the input space: a linear function, perhaps of a nonlinear feature map, or a kernel expansion. A decision tree does the opposite. It asks a sequence of yes/no questions about single features (“is the worst perimeter below 112.8?”), and the answer to each question decides which question comes next, so that different regions of the input space are described by different, simple rules. This chapter derives how such a tree is grown and pruned, why a single tree is a fragile model, and how averaging many trees (bagging and random forests) or adding them one after the other (boosting) turns it into one of the strongest general-purpose methods for tabular data.

11.1 Learning objectives¶

Chapter 4 ended with the observation that the best neighborhood for a point depends on the point, and Chapter 10 with the observation that the useful features depend on the region of the input space as well as on the problem. A decision tree builds both dependencies into the model: it chooses its neighborhoods and its features from the data, region by region. The price is a model with high variance, and the second half of the chapter is about how to remove that variance, or the bias, by combining many trees.

After working through the chapter you will be able to:

  1. write a regression tree as a piecewise-constant function on a partition of the feature space into boxes, prove that the best constant in each box is the mean of the targets, derive the gain of a split and the cost of finding it, and implement the greedy algorithm from scratch;

  2. define the impurity measures of classification (Gini index, entropy, misclassification rate), prove that every split of a concave impurity can only decrease it, and show that the Gini index is the squared error on one-hot targets;

  3. prune a tree by cost-complexity pruning, prove that the optimal subtrees form a nested sequence indexed by the penalty, and choose the penalty by cross-validation with the one-standard-error rule of Chapter 5;

  4. state the inductive bias of trees (invariance to monotone transformations of the features, adaptive neighborhoods, indifference to irrelevant features, axis-aligned boundaries) and measure it against the methods of the earlier chapters;

  5. prove that the variance of an average of correlated predictors is ρσ2+(1−ρ)σ2/B\rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/Bρσ2+(1−ρ)σ2/B, derive bagging, the out-of-bag estimate of the error and random forests, and measure ρ\rhoρ, σ2\sigma^2σ2 and the effect of the number of trees on real data;

  6. compute and interpret feature importances (impurity-based and permutation), and explain why they are biased, why correlated features share the credit, and how selection on importances leaks the labels when it is done outside the cross-validation loop;

  7. derive AdaBoost as stagewise minimization of the exponential loss and prove its bound on the training error; derive gradient boosting as gradient descent in a space of functions, with the Newton (second-order, regularized) leaf values and split gain used by modern implementations;

  8. explain why the probabilities of trees and ensembles must be recalibrated, and recalibrate them with Platt scaling (Section 8.7.3), and compare trees, forests and boosting with the linear, margin and kernel methods of the earlier chapters on the same three data sets with the same protocol.

We use the three data sets of Chapters 6 to 10 with the same splits: Diabetes (331/111331/111331/111 patients, regression), Breast Cancer (stratified 426/143426/143426/143, malignant =1=1=1, binary classification) and Digits (stratified 1347/4501347/4501347/450, ten classes). The test sets are touched only in Section 11.11, as in the other chapters; exploratory curves in the earlier sections use the training set or, when they are drawn on the test set to illustrate a point, say so, and when two implementations of the same algorithm are compared on the test inputs only their agreement is looked at, not their error.

11.2 Regression trees¶

11.2.1 Partitions and piecewise-constant functions¶

A decision tree is a way of writing a function that is constant on each box of a partition of the feature space.

Definition 11.1 (decision tree)

A binary decision tree on Rp\mathbb{R}^pRp is a rooted binary tree in which every internal node ttt carries a split (jt,st)(j_t, s_t)(jt​,st​), a feature index and a threshold, and has a left and a right child; every leaf mmm carries a prediction cmc_mcm​. An input x\mathbf{x}x is sent from the root to a leaf: at node ttt it goes left if xjt≤stx_{j_t}\le s_txjt​​≤st​ and right otherwise. The leaves correspond to boxes R1,…,RMR_1,\dots,R_MR1​,…,RM​ (products of intervals) that partition Rp\mathbb{R}^pRp, and the tree computes

fT(x)=∑m=1Mcm I[x∈Rm].f_T(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} c_m\,\mathbb{I}[\mathbf{x}\in R_m].fT​(x)=m=1∑M​cm​I[x∈Rm​].
(1)

The depth of a leaf is the number of splits on the path from the root, and ∣T∣=M\lvert T\rvert = M∣T∣=M is the number of leaves.

So a tree is a piecewise-constant function, and two things have to be chosen: the partition and the constants. The second choice is trivial.

Proposition 11.1 (the best constant in a box is the mean)

Given a partition R1,…,RMR_1,\dots,R_MR1​,…,RM​ and training data (xi,yi)(\mathbf{x}_i,y_i)(xi​,yi​), the constants that minimize the training squared error ∑i(yi−fT(xi))2\sum_i (y_i-f_T(\mathbf{x}_i))^2∑i​(yi​−fT​(xi​))2 are the means cm=yˉm=1nm∑i:xi∈Rmyic_m = \bar y_m = \frac1{n_m}\sum_{i:\mathbf{x}_i\in R_m}y_icm​=yˉ​m​=nm​1​∑i:xi​∈Rm​​yi​ of the targets that fall in each box (any cmc_mcm​ if the box is empty), and the minimal value is the residual sum of squares RSS(T)=∑mRSS(Rm)\mathrm{RSS}(T)=\sum_m \mathrm{RSS}(R_m)RSS(T)=∑m​RSS(Rm​) with RSS(Rm)=∑i∈Rm(yi−yˉm)2\mathrm{RSS}(R_m) = \sum_{i\in R_m}(y_i-\bar y_m)^2RSS(Rm​)=∑i∈Rm​​(yi​−yˉ​m​)2.

Proof. The sum splits into one sum per box, and in box mmm the quantity ∑i∈Rm(yi−c)2\sum_{i\in R_m}(y_i-c)^2∑i∈Rm​​(yi​−c)2 is a parabola in ccc whose derivative −2∑i∈Rm(yi−c)-2\sum_{i\in R_m}(y_i-c)−2∑i∈Rm​​(yi​−c) vanishes at c=yˉmc=\bar y_mc=yˉ​m​. ■\blacksquare■

The prediction at a new point is therefore the average of the targets of the training points that fall in the same box: a tree is a local average, exactly like kkk-NN regression in Chapter 4, with one difference that will matter throughout the chapter. The neighbors of x\mathbf{x}x are not the kkk nearest points in a fixed distance but the points that share a box with x\mathbf{x}x, and the boxes are learned from the targets.

11.2.2 Growing a tree: the gain of a split¶

Choosing the best partition into MMM boxes is a combinatorial problem that is NP-complete (Hyafil and Rivest, 1976), so every practical algorithm is greedy: start with all the data in one box (the root), find the single best split, and apply the same procedure recursively to the two parts. At a node with the data set DDD of size nnn a split (j,s)(j,s)(j,s) sends DL={i:xij≤s}D_L=\{i:x_{ij}\le s\}DL​={i:xij​≤s} to the left and DRD_RDR​ to the right, and by Proposition 11.1 the best constants in the new boxes are the means of the two parts. How much does the split reduce the residual sum of squares?

Proposition 11.2 (gain of a split)

Let DDD be split into DLD_LDL​ and DRD_RDR​ with sizes nL,nRn_L,n_RnL​,nR​, n=nL+nRn=n_L+n_Rn=nL​+nR​ and means yˉL,yˉR\bar y_L,\bar y_Ryˉ​L​,yˉ​R​. Then

RSS(D)−RSS(DL)−RSS(DR)  =  nLnRn (yˉL−yˉR)2  ≥  0.\mathrm{RSS}(D) - \mathrm{RSS}(D_L) - \mathrm{RSS}(D_R) \;=\; \frac{n_Ln_R}{n}\,(\bar y_L-\bar y_R)^2 \;\ge\; 0.RSS(D)−RSS(DL​)−RSS(DR​)=nnL​nR​​(yˉ​L​−yˉ​R​)2≥0.
(2)

Proof. The overall mean is yˉ=(nLyˉL+nRyˉR)/n\bar y = (n_L\bar y_L + n_R\bar y_R)/nyˉ​=(nL​yˉ​L​+nR​yˉ​R​)/n. For a part, ∑i∈DL(yi−yˉ)2=RSS(DL)+nL(yˉL−yˉ)2\sum_{i\in D_L}(y_i-\bar y)^2 = \mathrm{RSS}(D_L) + n_L(\bar y_L-\bar y)^2∑i∈DL​​(yi​−yˉ​)2=RSS(DL​)+nL​(yˉ​L​−yˉ​)2 (add and subtract yˉL\bar y_Lyˉ​L​; the cross term has zero sum). The same holds for DRD_RDR​, so the gain is nL(yˉL−yˉ)2+nR(yˉR−yˉ)2n_L(\bar y_L-\bar y)^2+n_R(\bar y_R-\bar y)^2nL​(yˉ​L​−yˉ​)2+nR​(yˉ​R​−yˉ​)2. Now yˉL−yˉ=nRn(yˉL−yˉR)\bar y_L-\bar y = \frac{n_R}{n}(\bar y_L-\bar y_R)yˉ​L​−yˉ​=nnR​​(yˉ​L​−yˉ​R​) and yˉR−yˉ=−nLn(yˉL−yˉR)\bar y_R-\bar y=-\frac{n_L}{n}(\bar y_L-\bar y_R)yˉ​R​−yˉ​=−nnL​​(yˉ​L​−yˉ​R​), and nLnR2n2+nRnL2n2=nLnR(nR+nL)n2=nLnRnn_L\frac{n_R^2}{n^2}+n_R\frac{n_L^2}{n^2} = \frac{n_Ln_R(n_R+n_L)}{n^2}=\frac{n_Ln_R}{n}nL​n2nR2​​+nR​n2nL2​​=n2nL​nR​(nR​+nL​)​=nnL​nR​​. ■\blacksquare■

A split can never hurt the training error, and the gain is the squared difference between the two means weighted by nLnR/nn_Ln_R/nnL​nR​/n: it is large for splits that separate groups with very different means, and the weight nLnR/nn_Ln_R/nnL​nR​/n (largest when the sizes are equal) prefers balanced splits to ones that cut off a few points. The best split of a node maximizes this gain over all features jjj and all thresholds sss. For one feature only the order of its values matters: the partition induced by sss changes only when sss crosses a data value, so it is enough to consider the n−1n-1n−1 midpoints between consecutive distinct sorted values.

Proposition 11.3 (cost of the search)

After sorting the values of one feature at a node of size nnn, the gains of all the n−1n-1n−1 candidate thresholds are computed in O(n)O(n)O(n) time from the prefix sums ∑i≤ky(i)\sum_{i\le k}y_{(i)}∑i≤k​y(i)​ and Proposition 11.2. The search over ppp features costs O(pnlog⁡n)O(pn\log n)O(pnlogn) at one node. Since every training point belongs to exactly one node of each depth, the cost of growing a tree up to depth DDD is O(Dpnlog⁡n)O(Dpn\log n)O(Dpnlogn).

Proof. With the sorted targets y(1),…,y(n)y_{(1)},\dots,y_{(n)}y(1)​,…,y(n)​ and prefix sums Sk=∑i≤ky(i)S_k=\sum_{i\le k}y_{(i)}Sk​=∑i≤k​y(i)​, a cut after position kkk has nL=kn_L=knL​=k, nR=n−kn_R=n-knR​=n−k, yˉL=Sk/k\bar y_L=S_k/kyˉ​L​=Sk​/k, yˉR=(Sn−Sk)/(n−k)\bar y_R=(S_n-S_k)/(n-k)yˉ​R​=(Sn​−Sk​)/(n−k), which Proposition 11.2 turns into the gain in constant time. Sorting costs O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) per feature, and the sum of the node sizes at one depth is at most nnn. ■\blacksquare■

(Implementations avoid most of the sorting by sorting each feature once, or by binning the features into at most 255 bins as the histogram-based algorithms of Section 11.9 do, which makes the cost of a level linear in nnn.) The following code implements the search of Proposition 11.3 and the greedy recursion of this section, and compares them with scikit-learn on Diabetes.

def as_f32(X):
    """scikit-learn casts the features to float32 before growing a tree: values closer than float32 resolution are ties.
    (Diabetes has such near-ties, created by the standardization of the original data, so we do the same.)"""
    return np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float32).astype(np.float64)


def best_split_feature(x, y, min_leaf=1):
    """Best threshold of ONE feature for the squared error (Propositions 11.2 and 11.3).

    Returns (gain, threshold), where gain = RSS(parent) - RSS(left) - RSS(right).
    """
    order = np.argsort(x, kind="stable")
    xs, ys = x[order], y[order]
    n = len(ys)
    prefix = np.cumsum(ys)                      # S_k for k = 1..n
    n_left = np.arange(1, n)                    # a cut after position k puts k points on the left
    n_right = n - n_left
    mean_left = prefix[:-1] / n_left
    mean_right = (prefix[-1] - prefix[:-1]) / n_right
    gain = n_left * n_right / n * (mean_left - mean_right) ** 2
    valid = (xs[:-1] < xs[1:]) & (n_left >= min_leaf) & (n_right >= min_leaf)   # cannot cut between equal values
    if not valid.any():
        return 0.0, None
    k = int(np.argmax(np.where(valid, gain, -np.inf)))
    return float(gain[k]), 0.5 * (xs[k] + xs[k + 1])


def grow(X, y, max_depth, min_leaf=1, depth=0):
    """Greedy recursive binary splitting; a node is a dictionary."""
    node = {"value": float(y.mean()), "n": len(y)}
    if depth == max_depth or len(y) < 2 * min_leaf or np.ptp(y) == 0:
        return node
    best = max((best_split_feature(X[:, j], y, min_leaf) + (j,) for j in range(X.shape[1])), key=lambda g: g[0])
    gain, thr, j = best
    if thr is None or gain <= 0:
        return node
    left = X[:, j] <= thr
    node.update(feature=j, threshold=thr, gain=gain,
                left=grow(X[left], y[left], max_depth, min_leaf, depth + 1),
                right=grow(X[~left], y[~left], max_depth, min_leaf, depth + 1))
    return node


def predict_tree(node, X):
    if "feature" not in node:
        return np.full(len(X), node["value"])
    out = np.empty(len(X))
    left = X[:, node["feature"]] <= node["threshold"]
    out[left] = predict_tree(node["left"], X[left])
    out[~left] = predict_tree(node["right"], X[~left])
    return out


def count_leaves(node):
    return 1 if "feature" not in node else count_leaves(node["left"]) + count_leaves(node["right"])


# 1. the root split of Diabetes: from scratch against scikit-learn
Xd_tr32, Xd_te32 = as_f32(Xd_tr), as_f32(Xd_te)
gains = [(*best_split_feature(Xd_tr32[:, j], yd_tr), diab_names[j]) for j in range(10)]
gains.sort(reverse=True)
print("best split of each feature at the root (gain = reduction of the RSS), best first:")
print(pd.DataFrame(gains, columns=["gain", "threshold", "feature"]).head(4).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.5g}"))
sk1 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=1, random_state=SEED).fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr)
print(f"scikit-learn root split: feature {diab_names[sk1.tree_.feature[0]]}, threshold {sk1.tree_.threshold[0]:.6f}")
rss_root = float(((yd_tr - yd_tr.mean()) ** 2).sum())
print(f"the best split removes {gains[0][0] / rss_root:.1%} of the residual sum of squares of the root ({rss_root:.4g})")

# 2. whole trees of depth 1..5: predictions of the from-scratch tree and of scikit-learn
rows = []
for depth in range(1, 6):
    mine = grow(Xd_tr32, yd_tr, depth)
    sk = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, random_state=SEED).fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr)
    rows.append({"depth": depth, "leaves (ours)": count_leaves(mine), "leaves (sklearn)": sk.get_n_leaves(),
                 "max |difference| of predictions": float(np.abs(predict_tree(mine, Xd_te32) - sk.predict(Xd_te)).max())})
print()
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.2g}"))


def first_differences(node, sk, idx, X, y, path="root"):
    """Walk the two depth-4 trees together and report the nodes where they choose different splits."""
    t = sk.tree_
    if "feature" not in node or t.children_left[idx] == -1:
        return
    if t.feature[idx] != node["feature"] or abs(t.threshold[idx] - node["threshold"]) > 1e-6:
        print(f"  node {path} ({len(y)} patients): ours {diab_names[node['feature']]} (gain {node['gain']:.2f}),"
              f" scikit-learn {diab_names[t.feature[idx]]} (gain {best_split_feature(X[:, t.feature[idx]], y)[0]:.2f})")
        return
    mask = X[:, node["feature"]] <= node["threshold"]
    first_differences(node["left"], sk, t.children_left[idx], X[mask], y[mask], path + "L")
    first_differences(node["right"], sk, t.children_right[idx], X[~mask], y[~mask], path + "R")


print("\nwhere do the depth-4 trees choose different splits?")
first_differences(grow(Xd_tr32, yd_tr, 4), DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=4, random_state=SEED).fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr), 0, Xd_tr32, yd_tr)

# 3. the cost of one search, as the number of points doubles (Proposition 11.3): the ratio of the times should be close to 2
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
times = []
for n in [20_000, 40_000, 80_000, 160_000]:
    x, y = rng.standard_normal(n), rng.standard_normal(n)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(5):
        best_split_feature(x, y)
    times.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) / 5)
print("\nratio of the time of one search when n doubles:", " ".join(f"{b / a:.1f}" for a, b in zip(times[:-1], times[1:])))

The code shows three things. First, the best split of each feature (the rows of the first table) and the winner agree with scikit-learn: the root of the Diabetes tree splits on the body mass index (bmi) at a threshold of 0.0051 (the features are in the standardized units of the data set), which removes 29.0%29.0\%29.0% of the residual sum of squares of the root in one step; the next best features are s5 and bp. Second, our recursion and scikit-learn produce the same predictions for depths 1, 2 and 3 (differences of 0). At depth 4 the two trees differ, and the last printed lines show why: in two small nodes (of 3 and 8 patients) two different splits have exactly the same gain, so that the greedy rule does not determine the tree; scikit-learn breaks such ties by a random permutation of the features (hence the argument random_state), our code takes the first. Both trees are legitimate outputs of the same greedy algorithm, and this will matter later: when several splits are equally good, the choice is arbitrary, and nearly equal splits make the tree unstable (Section 11.5). (A technical remark: scikit-learn converts the features to single precision before growing a tree, which turns the near-ties created by the standardization of Diabetes into exact ties; as_f32 does the same.) Third, the time of one search grows by a factor of about 2 to 2.5 when nnn doubles (the exact ratios depend on the machine), as the O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) of Proposition 11.3 predicts.

11.2.3 A worked example by hand¶

Worked example 11.1 (the first split of a six-point data set)

(Constructed data, to be checked by hand.) One feature, six points: x=(1,2,3,4,5,6)x=(1,2,3,4,5,6)x=(1,2,3,4,5,6) and y=(1,2,1,7,8,9)y=(1,2,1,7,8,9)y=(1,2,1,7,8,9). The sum of squares around the mean yˉ=28/6\bar y=28/6yˉ​=28/6 is RSS=∑yi2−6yˉ2=200−130.67=69.33\mathrm{RSS}=\sum y_i^2 - 6\bar y^2 = 200-130.67 = 69.33RSS=∑yi2​−6yˉ​2=200−130.67=69.33. x_ex = np.array([1., 2., 3., 4., 5., 6.])
y_ex = np.array([1., 2., 1., 7., 8., 9.])

    rows.append({"threshold": x_ex[k - 1] + 0.5, "n_L": k, "mean left": yl.mean(), "mean right": yr.mean(),
                 "gain (Prop. 11.2)": gain, "gain (direct RSS)": direct})
print(f"RSS of the root = {rss_total:.2f}")

11.2.4 What a tree looks like¶

Figure 11.1 shows regression trees on Diabetes. Panel (a) uses the single feature bmi: the fit is a staircase, with one step more for every extra split, and the full tree ends with one leaf per distinct value, interpolating the training points. Panel (b) uses two features, bmi and s5, and draws the partition of the plane into boxes made by a tree with 8 leaves: the lines are all horizontal or vertical, and each box carries one constant. The table printed before the figure gives the training and test error of trees of increasing depth (all features).

rows = []
for depth in [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, None]:
    t = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, random_state=SEED).fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr)
    rows.append({"max depth": "none" if depth is None else depth, "leaves": t.get_n_leaves(),
                 "train RMSE": rmse(t.predict(Xd_tr), yd_tr), "test RMSE": rmse(t.predict(Xd_te), yd_te)})
tree_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(tree_table.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.1f}"))
ols_d = LinearRegression().fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr)
print(f"\nreference (Chapter 6): constant prediction {rmse(np.full(len(yd_te), yd_tr.mean()), yd_te):.2f},"
      f" least squares {rmse(ols_d.predict(Xd_te), yd_te):.2f} (test RMSE)")


def figure_11_1():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.3))
    ax = axes[0]
    j = diab_names.index("bmi")
    xg = np.linspace(Xd_tr[:, j].min(), Xd_tr[:, j].max(), 600)
    ax.scatter(Xd_tr[:, j], yd_tr, s=9, color="0.65", label="training patients")
    for depth, color, ls in [(1, ORANGE, "-"), (2, GREEN, "-"), (4, BLUE, "-"), (None, VERMILION, ":")]:
        t = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, random_state=SEED).fit(Xd_tr[:, [j]], yd_tr)
        lab = "no limit" if depth is None else f"depth {depth}"
        ax.plot(xg, t.predict(xg[:, None]), color=color, ls=ls, lw=2 if depth else 1.2, label=f"{lab} ({t.get_n_leaves()} leaves)")
    ax.set_xlabel("body mass index (standardized, as in the data set)")

    g1 = np.linspace(Xd_tr[:, ja].min() - 0.01, Xd_tr[:, ja].max() + 0.01, 300)

    P = t.predict(np.c_[G1.ravel(), G2.ravel()]).reshape(G1.shape)
    im = ax.pcolormesh(G1, G2, P, cmap="cividis", shading="auto", alpha=0.85)

The table of the depth shows the pattern of this chapter. The training error falls steadily, from 65.5 with a single split to 0 for the tree with no limit, which has 324 leaves for 331 patients (almost one leaf per patient: the tree interpolates the data). The test error does not follow: it falls from 65.9 to 59.5 and 59.3 for depths 2 and 3, and then rises, to 66.7 at depth 6 and to 77.1 for the full tree, worse than the constant prediction of the mean (74.88) that ignores all the features. A tree that is too deep is a lookup table of the training set, with the high variance of a 1-nearest-neighbor rule, and the shallow tree that does best has a test RMSE of 59.3, against 53.37 for least squares (Chapter 6): on Diabetes a handful of boxes cannot match a linear model. (The numbers of the test set are used here to show the shape of the curve; choosing the depth by looking at them would be the mistake of Chapter 5, and Section 11.4 chooses the size of the tree by cross-validation.) In Figure 11.1(a) the same thing is visible as a staircase: depth 1 gives two levels, depth 2 gives four, depth 4 follows the cloud with sixteen steps, and the tree without limit jumps from one patient to the next. Panel (b) shows the partition that a tree with 8 leaves makes of the plane of two features: every boundary is parallel to an axis, and the prediction increases with both the body mass index and the triglycerides.

11.3 Classification trees and impurity¶

11.3.1 Node impurity¶

For a classification problem with KKK classes the leaf mmm holds the class proportions p^mk=1nm#{i∈Rm:yi=k}\hat p_{mk}=\frac1{n_m}\#\{i\in R_m:y_i=k\}p^​mk​=nm​1​#{i∈Rm​:yi​=k}, predicts the majority class, and may report p^mk\hat p_{mk}p^​mk​ as its estimate of P(y=k∣x∈Rm)\mathbb{P}(y=k\mid\mathbf{x}\in R_m)P(y=k∣x∈Rm​) (we shall see in Section 11.10 that this estimate is poor). The squared error of the regression tree is replaced by a measure of how mixed a node is.

Definition 11.2 (impurity)

An impurity is a function φ\varphiφ of the class proportions p^=(p^1,…,p^K)\hat{\mathbf{p}}=(\hat p_1,\dots,\hat p_K)p^​=(p^​1​,…,p^​K​), concave on the simplex, symmetric in its arguments and zero at the vertices (a pure node). The three standard ones are

misclassification rate:  1−max⁡kp^k,Gini index:  G=∑kp^k(1−p^k)=1−∑kp^k2,entropy:  H=−∑kp^kln⁡p^k.\text{misclassification rate: }\ 1-\max_k\hat p_k,\qquad \text{Gini index: }\ G=\sum_{k}\hat p_k(1-\hat p_k)=1-\sum_k\hat p_k^2,\qquad \text{entropy: }\ H=-\sum_k\hat p_k\ln\hat p_k .misclassification rate:  1−kmax​p^​k​,Gini index:  G=k∑​p^​k​(1−p^​k​)=1−k∑​p^​k2​,entropy:  H=−k∑​p^​k​lnp^​k​.
(3)

The gain of a split of a node DDD into DL,DRD_L,D_RDL​,DR​ is Δφ=φ(p^D)−nLnφ(p^L)−nRnφ(p^R)\Delta\varphi=\varphi(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_D)-\frac{n_L}{n}\varphi(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_L)-\frac{n_R}{n}\varphi(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_R)Δφ=φ(p^​D​)−nnL​​φ(p^​L​)−nnR​​φ(p^​R​), and the tree is grown by maximizing it, exactly as in the regression case.

Proposition 11.4 (a split never increases a concave impurity)

For every concave φ\varphiφ and every split, Δφ≥0\Delta\varphi\ge 0Δφ≥0. If φ\varphiφ is strictly concave, Δφ=0\Delta\varphi=0Δφ=0 only if p^L=p^R\hat{\mathbf{p}}_L=\hat{\mathbf{p}}_Rp^​L​=p^​R​, that is, only if the split does not change the class proportions.

Proof. The proportions of the parent are the weighted average p^D=nLnp^L+nRnp^R\hat{\mathbf{p}}_D=\frac{n_L}{n}\hat{\mathbf{p}}_L+\frac{n_R}{n}\hat{\mathbf{p}}_Rp^​D​=nnL​​p^​L​+nnR​​p^​R​ of those of the children, so Jensen’s inequality for the concave φ\varphiφ gives φ(p^D)≥nLnφ(p^L)+nRnφ(p^R)\varphi(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_D)\ge\frac{n_L}{n}\varphi(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_L)+\frac{n_R}{n}\varphi(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_R)φ(p^​D​)≥nnL​​φ(p^​L​)+nnR​​φ(p^​R​), with equality for strictly concave φ\varphiφ only if the two points coincide. ■\blacksquare■

The Gini index and the entropy are strictly concave, but the misclassification rate is only piecewise linear: it is not strictly concave, and it can give a gain of exactly zero to a split that has made the node visibly purer. The standard example has 400 examples of each of two classes. Split A produces two children with (300,100)(300,100)(300,100) and (100,300)(100,300)(100,300) examples of the two classes; split B produces (200,400)(200,400)(200,400) and (200,0)(200,0)(200,0). Both misclassify 200 of the 800 examples, so the misclassification rate cannot tell them apart, although B has isolated a pure node and A has not.

def impurities(counts):
    """Misclassification rate, Gini index and entropy (nats) from a vector of class counts."""
    p = np.asarray(counts, float) / np.sum(counts)
    nz = p[p > 0]
    return 1 - p.max(), 1 - np.sum(p ** 2), -np.sum(nz * np.log(nz))


def split_gain(parent, left, right):
    n, nl, nr = np.sum(parent), np.sum(left), np.sum(right)
    return [impurities(parent)[i] - nl / n * impurities(left)[i] - nr / n * impurities(right)[i] for i in range(3)]


parent = (400, 400)
rows = []
for name, (left, right) in {"A: (300,100) + (100,300)": ((300, 100), (100, 300)),
                            "B: (200,400) + (200,0)": ((200, 400), (200, 0))}.items():
    g = split_gain(parent, left, right)
    rows.append({"split": name, "misclassification": g[0], "Gini": g[1], "entropy": g[2]})
print("gain of the two splits of a node with (400, 400) examples:")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
gain of the two splits of a node with (400, 400) examples:
                   split  misclassification   Gini  entropy
A: (300,100) + (100,300)             0.2500 0.1250   0.1308
  B: (200,400) + (200,0)             0.2500 0.1667   0.2158

The two splits have the same misclassification gain (0.25), because both leave 200 of the 800 examples misclassified, but B has the larger gain in the Gini index (0.1667 against 0.1250) and in the entropy (0.2158 against 0.1308), as it should: the pure node of B can be left alone, and the other node has only one more split to make. The strictly concave impurities reward progress that is not yet visible in the error rate, and this is why trees are grown with the Gini index or the entropy and not with the misclassification rate, which is nevertheless often the criterion used to prune (Section 11.4).

11.3.2 Gini is a squared error¶

The Gini index has a second interpretation that links this section to the previous one. Code the class of the iii-th example as the one-hot vector eyi∈{0,1}K\mathbf{e}_{y_i}\in\{0,1\}^Keyi​​∈{0,1}K.

Proposition 11.5 (Gini = squared error on one-hot targets)

For a node with nnn examples and class proportions p^\hat{\mathbf{p}}p^​, the residual sum of squares of the one-hot targets around their mean p^\hat{\mathbf{p}}p^​ is ∑i∥eyi−p^∥2=n G(p^)\sum_i\lVert\mathbf{e}_{y_i}-\hat{\mathbf{p}}\rVert^2=n\,G(\hat{\mathbf{p}})∑i​∥eyi​​−p^​∥2=nG(p^​). Hence the gain of a split in the Gini index, multiplied by nnn, is the gain of Proposition 11.2 summed over the KKK coordinates of the one-hot target: a classification tree grown with the Gini index is a regression tree for the one-hot targets, and a leaf’s class proportions are the means of the targets in the box (Proposition 11.1).

Proof. ∥eyi−p^∥2=1−2p^yi+∑kp^k2\lVert\mathbf{e}_{y_i}-\hat{\mathbf{p}}\rVert^2 = 1-2\hat p_{y_i}+\sum_k\hat p_k^2∥eyi​​−p^​∥2=1−2p^​yi​​+∑k​p^​k2​, and summing over iii, ∑ip^yi=∑knp^kp^k=n∑kp^k2\sum_i\hat p_{y_i}=\sum_k n\hat p_k\hat p_k = n\sum_k\hat p_k^2∑i​p^​yi​​=∑k​np^​k​p^​k​=n∑k​p^​k2​, so the total is n−2n∑p^k2+n∑p^k2=n(1−∑kp^k2)n-2n\sum\hat p_k^2+n\sum\hat p_k^2 = n(1-\sum_k\hat p_k^2)n−2n∑p^​k2​+n∑p^​k2​=n(1−∑k​p^​k2​). The statement on the gain follows because Proposition 11.2 holds coordinate by coordinate. ■\blacksquare■

This is why the regression tree of Section 11.2 and the classification tree of this section are one algorithm, and why the probability estimates of a leaf are means (and carry the problems of means of few numbers, Section 11.10). The next cell checks the proposition on the root of the Breast Cancer tree, and shows how the three criteria rank the thresholds of the feature that the tree uses at the root.

def best_split_gini(x, y, K=2):
    """Best threshold of one feature for the Gini index, from the class counts to the left of each cut."""
    order = np.argsort(x, kind="stable")
    xs, ys = x[order], y[order]
    n = len(ys)
    onehot = np.eye(K)[ys]
    left = np.cumsum(onehot, axis=0)[:-1]                       # class counts on the left, for each cut
    right = onehot.sum(axis=0) - left
    nl, nr = left.sum(axis=1), right.sum(axis=1)
    g_left = 1 - ((left / nl[:, None]) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
    g_right = 1 - ((right / nr[:, None]) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
    g_parent = 1 - ((onehot.sum(axis=0) / n) ** 2).sum()
    gain = g_parent - (nl * g_left + nr * g_right) / n
    gain = np.where(xs[:-1] < xs[1:], gain, -np.inf)
    k = int(np.argmax(gain))
    return float(gain[k]), 0.5 * (xs[k] + xs[k + 1]), xs, gain


# the root split of the Breast Cancer tree, found by three routes
res = [(bc_names[j], *best_split_gini(Xb_tr[:, j], yb_tr)[:2]) for j in range(30)]
res.sort(key=lambda r: -r[1])
print("best Gini gain per feature (top 3):")
print(pd.DataFrame(res[:3], columns=["feature", "Gini gain", "threshold"]).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
sk_c = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=SEED).fit(Xb_tr, yb_tr)
print(f"scikit-learn root: {bc_names[sk_c.tree_.feature[0]]} <= {sk_c.tree_.threshold[0]:.4f}")

# Proposition 11.5: n * (Gini gain) equals the sum over the two coordinates of the one-hot target of the RSS gain of Proposition 11.2
j_root = bc_names.index(res[0][0])
n_b = len(yb_tr)

The three routes agree: the root of the Breast Cancer tree splits on the worst perimeter at 112.8 (a Gini gain of 0.3369), and nnn times the Gini gain, 143.540228, equals the sum of the two squared-error gains on the one-hot targets to all printed digits, as Proposition 11.5 says. def figure_11_2():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.1))
    ax = axes[0]
    p = np.linspace(0, 1, 401)
    ax.plot(p, np.minimum(p, 1 - p), color=BLUE, lw=2, label="misclassification rate")
    ax.plot(p, 2 * p * (1 - p), color=ORANGE, lw=2, ls="--", label=r"Gini index $2p(1-p)$")
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
        ent = -(p * np.log2(p) + (1 - p) * np.log2(1 - p)) / 2
    ax.plot(p, np.nan_to_num(ent), color=GREEN, lw=2, ls=":", label="entropy in bits, halved")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"proportion $\hat p$ of class 1 in the node")
    ax.set_ylabel("impurity")
    ax.set_title("(a) two classes: three concave impurities")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)

    ax = axes[1]
    j = bc_names.index("worst perimeter")
    order = np.argsort(Xb_tr[:, j])
    xs, ys = Xb_tr[order, j], yb_tr[order]
    n = len(ys)
    cum1 = np.cumsum(ys)[:-1]
    nl = np.arange(1, n)
    nr = n - nl
    p1_l, p1_r = cum1 / nl, (ys.sum() - cum1) / nr
    p1 = ys.mean()
    g = lambda q: 2 * q * (1 - q)
    m = lambda q: np.minimum(q, 1 - q)
    gain_gini = g(p1) - (nl * g(p1_l) + nr * g(p1_r)) / n
    gain_mis = m(p1) - (nl * m(p1_l) + nr * m(p1_r)) / n
    mid = 0.5 * (xs[:-1] + xs[1:])
    ok = xs[:-1] < xs[1:]
    ax.plot(mid[ok], gain_gini[ok], color=ORANGE, lw=1.8, ls="--", label="Gini gain")
    ax.plot(mid[ok], gain_mis[ok], color=BLUE, lw=1.8, label="misclassification gain")
    ax.axvline(mid[ok][np.argmax(gain_gini[ok])], color="0.4", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("threshold on worst perimeter")
    ax.set_ylabel("gain of the split of the root")
    ax.set_title("(b) Breast Cancer: the root split")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig


figure_11_2()
plt.show()

Figure 11.2 summarizes the section. Panel (a) shows the three impurities for two classes: the Gini index and the entropy are smooth and strictly concave, the misclassification rate is a tent. Panel (b) shows the criteria as functions of the threshold for the root split of Breast Cancer. All have their maximum at 112.8, but the misclassification gain is exactly zero for the first 107 of the 398 candidate thresholds, up to 84.4: for all of them the left child is pure (benign) and the right child still has a benign majority, so that the predictions are those of the root and the error rate does not move, while the Gini gain has already reached 0.095. A greedy algorithm driven by the error rate would see nothing to gain from isolating a pure node.

11.4 Controlling the size of a tree: cost-complexity pruning¶

11.4.1 Stopping early or growing and pruning¶

Section 11.2 showed that a tree grown to purity memorizes the training set. The simplest remedy is to stop growing early: a maximum depth, a minimum number of examples in a leaf (min_samples_leaf), or a minimum gain for a split. These rules are easy to state but short-sighted: a split with a small gain may open the way to a split with a large gain (the exclusive-or pattern is the standard example: no single split of x1x_1x1​ or x2x_2x2​ reduces the impurity, and the two together separate the classes perfectly). The method of Breiman, Friedman, Olshen and Stone (1984), called CART, therefore grows a deliberately large tree and then removes the splits that are not worth their cost.

11.4.2 The pruning criterion and the nested sequence of optimal subtrees¶

Let T0T_0T0​ be the large tree. A pruned subtree T⪯T0T\preceq T_0T⪯T0​ is obtained by collapsing some internal nodes into leaves (together with everything below them). Write R(m)R(m)R(m) for the cost of the node mmm when it is a leaf: its residual sum of squares divided by nnn in regression, its weighted impurity in classification (the impurity of the node times the fraction of the training set that reaches it), and R(T)=∑m∈leaves(T)R(m)R(T)=\sum_{m\in\text{leaves}(T)}R(m)R(T)=∑m∈leaves(T)​R(m) for the training cost of the tree. A pruned subtree has a larger cost than T0T_0T0​ (Propositions 11.2 and 11.4), and it has fewer leaves. The cost-complexity criterion puts a price α≥0\alpha\ge0α≥0 on every leaf:

Rα(T)=R(T)+α ∣T∣.(11.1)R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha\,\lvert T\rvert . \tag{11.1}Rα​(T)=R(T)+α∣T∣.(11.1)
(4)

For α=0\alpha=0α=0 the best subtree is the full tree, for large α\alphaα it is the root alone. Among the exponentially many subtrees, how should we find the best one for each α\alphaα, and how do these best subtrees depend on α\alphaα? The answer is as clean as one could hope.

Proposition 11.6 (the optimal subtrees are nested)

For every α≥0\alpha\ge0α≥0 the criterion (11.1) has a unique smallest minimizer T(α)⪯T0T(\alpha)\preceq T_0T(α)⪯T0​ (smallest in the number of leaves). The tree T(α)T(\alpha)T(α) can be computed by a single bottom-up pass, and

α<α′ ⟹ T(α′)⪯T(α).\alpha<\alpha'\ \Longrightarrow\ T(\alpha')\preceq T(\alpha).α<α′ ⟹ T(α′)⪯T(α).
(5)

Consequently there are at most ∣T0∣−1\lvert T_0\rvert-1∣T0​∣−1 distinct optimal subtrees, with break points 0=α0<α1<…0=\alpha_0<\alpha_1<\dots0=α0​<α1​<…; the next subtree is obtained from the current one by collapsing the weakest link, the internal node ttt that minimizes g(t)=R(t)−R(Tt)∣Tt∣−1g(t)=\dfrac{R(t)-R(T_t)}{\lvert T_t\rvert-1}g(t)=∣Tt​∣−1R(t)−R(Tt​)​, where TtT_tTt​ is the part of the current tree below ttt.

Proof. For a node ttt of T0T_0T0​ with children l,rl,rl,r, let Cα(t)C_\alpha(t)Cα​(t) be the minimum of RαR_\alphaRα​ over the pruned subtrees of the tree TtT_tTt​ rooted at ttt. A pruned subtree of TtT_tTt​ is either the single leaf ttt, with cost R(t)+αR(t)+\alphaR(t)+α, or the node ttt with a pruned subtree on each side, so that Cα(t)=min⁡{R(t)+α, Cα(l)+Cα(r)}C_\alpha(t)=\min\{R(t)+\alpha,\ C_\alpha(l)+C_\alpha(r)\}Cα​(t)=min{R(t)+α, Cα​(l)+Cα​(r)}, and Cα(t)=R(t)+αC_\alpha(t)=R(t)+\alphaCα​(t)=R(t)+α at a leaf. This recursion computes the optimum from the leaves up; collapsing at ttt is optimal exactly when the function

Φt(α)=Cα(l)+Cα(r)−R(t)−α\Phi_t(\alpha)=C_\alpha(l)+C_\alpha(r)-R(t)-\alphaΦt​(α)=Cα​(l)+Cα​(r)−R(t)−α
(6)

is ≥0\ge0≥0. Each Cα(u)C_\alpha(u)Cα​(u) is a minimum of functions R(T′)+α∣T′∣R(T')+\alpha\lvert T'\rvertR(T′)+α∣T′∣, so Φt(α)=min⁡Tl′,Tr′[R(Tl′)+R(Tr′)−R(t)]+α(∣Tl′∣+∣Tr′∣−1)\Phi_t(\alpha)=\min_{T_l',T_r'}\big[R(T_l')+R(T_r')-R(t)\big]+\alpha\big(\lvert T_l'\rvert+\lvert T_r'\rvert-1\big)Φt​(α)=minTl′​,Tr′​​[R(Tl′​)+R(Tr′​)−R(t)]+α(∣Tl′​∣+∣Tr′​∣−1) is a minimum of affine functions of α\alphaα whose slopes are all ≥1\ge1≥1: it is strictly increasing. At α=0\alpha=0α=0 the minimum is attained by the unpruned subtrees, and Φt(0)=R(Tl)+R(Tr)−R(t)≤0\Phi_t(0)=R(T_l)+R(T_r)-R(t)\le0Φt​(0)=R(Tl​)+R(Tr​)−R(t)≤0 by the monotonicity of the cost. So Φt\Phi_tΦt​ has exactly one zero αt≥0\alpha_t\ge0αt​≥0, and collapsing ttt is optimal (we collapse at ties, to get the smallest tree) if and only if α≥αt\alpha\ge\alpha_tα≥αt​. Going down from the root, T(α)T(\alpha)T(α) keeps the split at ttt as long as α<αt′\alpha<\alpha_{t'}α<αt′​ for every node t′t't′ on the path from the root to ttt, and collapses at the first node where α≥αt′\alpha\ge\alpha_{t'}α≥αt′​: an internal node of T(α)T(\alpha)T(α) must satisfy α<αt′\alpha<\alpha_{t'}α<αt′​ for all its ancestors and itself, which becomes harder as α\alphaα grows, so the set of internal nodes can only shrink. Finally, at the break point of ttt the cost of collapsing it equals the cost of the current optimal subtree below it, R(t)+α=R(Tt)+α∣Tt∣R(t)+\alpha=R(T_t)+\alpha\lvert T_t\rvertR(t)+α=R(Tt​)+α∣Tt​∣, and solving for α\alphaα gives g(t)g(t)g(t). ■\blacksquare■

The proof used only the fact that splitting does not increase the cost, so it holds for any node cost that satisfies Propositions 11.2 or 11.4 (squared error, Gini, entropy, misclassification count); scikit-learn uses the node impurity of the criterion with which the tree was grown. The weakest-link formula is also the algorithm: compute g(t)g(t)g(t) for every internal node, collapse the node with the smallest value (all the ties together), record it as the next break point, and repeat. The next cell implements it and compares the break points and the sizes of the subtrees with cost_complexity_pruning_path and ccp_alpha of scikit-learn, on the full Diabetes tree.

def weakest_link_path(fitted_tree):
    """Cost-complexity pruning from scratch (Proposition 11.6): break points alpha_k and numbers of leaves of T(alpha_k)."""
    T = fitted_tree.tree_
    left, right = T.children_left, T.children_right
    R = T.impurity * T.weighted_n_node_samples / T.weighted_n_node_samples[0]      # R(m): impurity of the node times its share of the data
    is_leaf = left == -1                                                            # collapsed nodes are turned into leaves below

    def subtree_stats():
        R_sub, n_sub = np.zeros(T.node_count), np.zeros(T.node_count)
        for t in range(T.node_count - 1, -1, -1):                                   # children have larger indices than parents
            if is_leaf[t]:
                R_sub[t], n_sub[t] = R[t], 1
            else:
                R_sub[t], n_sub[t] = R_sub[left[t]] + R_sub[right[t]], n_sub[left[t]] + n_sub[right[t]]
        return R_sub, n_sub

    def reachable_internal():
        stack, out = [0], []
        while stack:
            t = stack.pop()
            if not is_leaf[t]:
                out.append(t)
                stack += [left[t], right[t]]
        return out

    alphas, leaves = [0.0], [int(subtree_stats()[1][0])]
    while not is_leaf[0]:
        R_sub, n_sub = subtree_stats()
        internal = reachable_internal()
        g = {t: (R[t] - R_sub[t]) / (n_sub[t] - 1) for t in internal}
        g_min = min(g.values())
        for t in internal:
            if g[t] <= g_min * (1 + 1e-9) + 1e-300:
                is_leaf[t] = True                                                   # collapse the weakest link (and ties)
        alphas.append(max(g_min, alphas[-1]))
        leaves.append(int(subtree_stats()[1][0]))
    return np.array(alphas), np.array(leaves)


def distinct(a, rtol=1e-9):
    """Sorted values, merging those that differ only by rounding errors."""
    a = np.sort(np.asarray(a, float))
    keep = [a[0]]
    for v in a[1:]:
        if v - keep[-1] > rtol * max(1.0, abs(v)):
            keep.append(v)
    return np.array(keep)


full_d = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=SEED).fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr)
a_mine, leaves_mine = weakest_link_path(full_d)
a_sk = distinct(full_d.cost_complexity_pruning_path(Xd_tr, yd_tr).ccp_alphas)
a_mine_u = distinct(a_mine)
print(f"full tree: {full_d.get_n_leaves()} leaves.  Distinct break points: ours {len(a_mine_u)}, scikit-learn {len(a_sk)};"
      f"  largest difference {np.abs(a_mine_u - a_sk).max():.1e}")
leaves_sk = [DecisionTreeRegressor(ccp_alpha=a * (1 + 1e-9), random_state=SEED).fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr).get_n_leaves() for a in a_mine]   # a node is pruned when its g(t) <= alpha
print(f"number of leaves of the optimal subtree at each break point: identical to scikit-learn in "

The break points computed from the weakest-link formula agree with those of scikit-learn (the largest difference is 1.8×10−121.8\times10^{-12}1.8×10−12, rounding error), and so do the sizes of the optimal subtrees, in all 225 cases. The table shows how little most of the tree is worth. The unpruned tree has 324 leaves; a price of α=0.34\alpha=0.34α=0.34 per leaf (the unit of α\alphaα is that of RRR, here the mean squared error in squared units of the target) already removes 120 of them, and α=36\alpha=36α=36 leaves 32; the 3-leaf tree is optimal up to α=404\alpha=404α=404 and the root alone for α≥1756\alpha\ge1756α≥1756. A single pass over the nested sequence gives all the candidates, so cross-validating α\alphaα costs one tree fit per fold and per value, not a search over subtrees.

11.4.3 Choosing α\alphaα by cross-validation¶

The parameter α\alphaα is the one hyperparameter of the pruned tree, and it is chosen like all the others, by KKK-fold cross-validation (Chapter 5): for each value of α\alphaα a tree is grown on the training part of each fold and pruned with that α\alphaα, and the error is measured on the validation part. We use the break points of the full tree as the grid (a different value between two break points gives the same subtree) and the one-standard-error rule of Section 5.4.1 and Section 10.7.1: take the smallest tree whose cross-validated error is within one standard error of the minimum. The grid for Diabetes has 224 values and each is evaluated with 10 folds, 2,2402{,}2402,240 tree fits in all (the last break point, which leaves only the root, is left out, and we compare with the constant prediction instead).

def cv_over_alphas(make_tree, X, y, alphas, cv, scoring):
    """Cross-validated error for a grid of ccp_alpha values: mean and standard error over the folds."""
    rows = []
    for a in alphas:
        s = -cross_val_score(make_tree(a), X, y, cv=cv, scoring=scoring)
        rows.append((a, s.mean(), s.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(s))))
    return np.array(rows)


def one_se_choice(cv_table):
    """Index of the CV minimum and of the largest alpha (smallest tree) within one SE of it."""
    i_min = int(np.argmin(cv_table[:, 1]))
    ok = np.where(cv_table[:, 1] <= cv_table[i_min, 1] + cv_table[i_min, 2])[0]
    return i_min, int(ok.max())


kf10 = KFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
skf10 = StratifiedKFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)

# Diabetes: regression tree, squared error

train_rmse_d = np.array([rmse(DecisionTreeRegressor(ccp_alpha=a, random_state=SEED).fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr).predict(Xd_tr), yd_tr) for a in a_grid])

Figure 11.3 draws the two curves against the number of leaves, with the training error that decreases monotonically all the way down to zero while the cross-validated error has a shallow minimum. Figure 11.4 shows the pruned tree for Breast Cancer, which can be read as a short list of rules: tumors with a worst perimeter of at most 112.8 are benign unless the worst concave points exceed 0.18 (all 8 such tumors are malignant); among the 149 tumors with a larger perimeter, 139 are malignant, and so on. The tree has 9 splits and uses 7 of the 30 features, each one a threshold on a single measurement, and readability is the main reason trees are used at all: a clinician can follow it without a computer. Its weak point is also visible: several leaves hold a handful of patients (2, 4, 5), and the label of a leaf with 5 patients is a statistic of 5 numbers.

11.5 What a tree assumes: the inductive bias¶

Chapter 3 introduced the inductive bias of a learning method: the assumptions that make it work on some problems and fail on others, and the table at the end of Chapter 3 listed for trees “the label depends on a few features through simple threshold rules”. This section turns that sentence into five measurable statements.

11.5.1 Invariance to monotone transformations of the features¶

Every split of a tree compares one feature with a threshold, and the gain of Section 11.2 depends only on which training points go to the left. The set of such partitions for the feature xjx_jxj​ depends only on the order of its values.

Proposition 11.7 (invariance)

Let g1,…,gpg_1,\dots,g_pg1​,…,gp​ be strictly increasing functions and let the tree be grown on the transformed features gj(xij)g_j(x_{ij})gj​(xij​) instead of xijx_{ij}xij​. Then the greedy algorithm finds the same sequence of partitions of the training points (the same gains, the same leaves, the same predictions on the training points), up to the tie-breaking of Section 11.2.2. On new points the two trees can differ only for points that fall between two consecutive training values of the feature of a split, because the threshold is the midpoint of the two values in the coordinates in which the tree is grown, and gjg_jgj​ does not map midpoints to midpoints.

Proof. A strictly increasing gjg_jgj​ preserves the order and the ties of the values of feature jjj, so the family of sets {i:gj(xij)≤s}\{i: g_j(x_{ij})\le s\}{i:gj​(xij​)≤s}, s∈Rs\in\mathbb{R}s∈R, is the same family of subsets of the training points as {i:xij≤s}\{i:x_{ij}\le s\}{i:xij​≤s}. The gain of a split depends only on the subset, so the best split at each node is the same, and so is the recursion. For a new point x\mathbf{x}x, the decisions of the two trees at a node can differ only if xjx_jxj​ lies between the two consecutive training values that define the threshold, since for xjx_jxj​ outside that interval the comparison with the threshold is decided by the order. ■\blacksquare■

This is the fulfilment of a promise made in Section 2.7.1 and again in Section 9.6.4 and Exercise 9.8: a tree needs no standardization and no transformation of the features, and a skewed feature (an area, a concentration) can be given to it as it is. The next cell checks the statement on Breast Cancer, where the features have scales that differ by a factor of 104, and contrasts it with a nearest-neighbor rule and a logistic regression, which depend on the scale.

sc_b = StandardScaler().fit(Xb_tr)
variants = {"raw": (Xb_tr, Xb_te),
            "standardized": (sc_b.transform(Xb_tr), sc_b.transform(Xb_te)),
            "logarithm of 1 + x": (np.log1p(Xb_tr), np.log1p(Xb_te))}

# (i) the tree grown with the same gains: the splitting features, the impurities and the predictions
trees = {k: DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=SEED).fit(a, yb_tr) for k, (a, _) in variants.items()}
ref = trees["raw"]
for k, t in trees.items():
    same_struct = np.array_equal(t.tree_.feature, ref.tree_.feature) and np.allclose(t.tree_.impurity, ref.tree_.impurity)
    diff_test = int((t.predict(variants[k][1]) != ref.predict(Xb_te)).sum())
    print(f"{k:20s} same splitting features and impurities as the raw tree: {same_struct};  test predictions that differ: {diff_test} of {len(yb_te)}")

# (ii) 10-fold cross-validated accuracy on the training set of three methods under the three transformations
rows = []
for name, make in [("decision tree", lambda: DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=SEED)),
                   ("5-NN (no scaler)", lambda: KNeighborsClassifier(5)),
                   ("logistic regression, C=1 (no scaler)", lambda: LogisticRegression(C=1, max_iter=5000))]:
    row = {"method": name}
    for k, (a, _) in variants.items():
        row[k] = cross_val_score(make(), a, yb_tr, cv=skf10).mean()
    rows.append(row)
print()
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))

                       decision tree 0.9295        0.9295              0.9271
                    5-NN (no scaler) 0.9341        0.9553              0.9485
logistic regression, C=1 (no scaler) 0.9483        0.9789              0.9460

The three trees have the same splitting features and the same impurities, and none of the 143 test predictions differs, as Proposition 11.7 says: a feature in the units of the data, standardized, or compressed by a logarithm gives the same tree. The cross-validated accuracy of the tree is the same for the raw and the standardized features (0.9295) and differs slightly for the logarithm (0.9271): the proposition allows a difference for validation points that fall between two consecutive training values, and here a few of them do. The two other methods, in contrast, depend on the transformation: for 5-NN the cross-validated accuracy goes from 0.934 (raw) to 0.955 (standardized), and for the logistic regression, whose penalty acts unevenly on features of different scales, from 0.948 to 0.979. Invariance is a convenience, not a measure of quality: on this data the tree is less accurate than both of them (0.93 against 0.955 and 0.979 with standardized features).

11.5.2 Adaptive neighborhoods: a tree is a kkk-NN rule whose kkk depends on the point¶

Section 11.2.1 observed that a tree predicts by averaging the targets of the training points in the same box, as kkk-NN does, but with neighborhoods learned from the targets. The consequence is easy to see on two constructed regression problems with one feature, x∼U[0,1]x\sim\mathrm{U}[0,1]x∼U[0,1], n=100n=100n=100 and noise σ=0.3\sigma=0.3σ=0.3 as in Chapter 4: a step, f(x)=I[x>0.5]f(x)=\mathbb{I}[x>0.5]f(x)=I[x>0.5], and a smooth function, f(x)=sin⁡(2πx)f(x)=\sin(2\pi x)f(x)=sin(2πx). For each draw of the data we choose kkk for kkk-NN and α\alphaα for the tree by 5-fold cross-validation, and we measure the mean squared error against the true function fff on a grid. Near the jump a good neighborhood is narrow and on each side of it wide; a smooth function wants neighborhoods of similar size everywhere.

def one_world(f, rep, n=100, sigma=0.3):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1000 + rep)
    x = rng.uniform(0, 1, n)
    y = f(x) + sigma * rng.standard_normal(n)
    grid = np.linspace(0.005, 0.995, 200)
    kf = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=rep)
    ks = [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40]
    cv_k = [-cross_val_score(KNeighborsRegressor(k), x[:, None], y, cv=kf, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error").mean() for k in ks]
    k_best = ks[int(np.argmin(cv_k))]
    knn = KNeighborsRegressor(k_best).fit(x[:, None], y)
    path = distinct(DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0).fit(x[:, None], y).cost_complexity_pruning_path(x[:, None], y).ccp_alphas)
    alphas = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.geomspace(1e-4 * path.max(), path.max(), 20)])
    cv_a = [-cross_val_score(DecisionTreeRegressor(ccp_alpha=a, random_state=0), x[:, None], y, cv=kf, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error").mean() for a in alphas]
    tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(ccp_alpha=alphas[int(np.argmin(cv_a))], random_state=0).fit(x[:, None], y)
    return {"x": x, "y": y, "grid": grid, "knn": knn.predict(grid[:, None]), "tree": tree.predict(grid[:, None]),
            "mse_knn": float(np.mean((knn.predict(grid[:, None]) - f(grid)) ** 2)),
            "mse_tree": float(np.mean((tree.predict(grid[:, None]) - f(grid)) ** 2)), "k": k_best, "leaves": tree.get_n_leaves()}


worlds = {"step": lambda x: (x > 0.5) * 1.0, "sine": lambda x: np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)}
sim, rows = {}, []
for name, f in worlds.items():
    runs = [one_world(f, r) for r in range(40)]
    sim[name] = runs
    d = np.array([r["mse_tree"] - r["mse_knn"] for r in runs])
    rows.append({"true function": name, "k-NN MSE": np.mean([r["mse_knn"] for r in runs]), "tree MSE": np.mean([r["mse_tree"] for r in runs]),
                 "tree - kNN (mean)": d.mean(), "SE": d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(d)),
                 "mean k": np.mean([r["k"] for r in runs]), "mean leaves": np.mean([r["leaves"] for r in runs])})
print("40 constructed data sets of n = 100 per world; k-NN and the tree are tuned by 5-fold CV on each")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
40 constructed data sets of n = 100 per world; k-NN and the tree are tuned by 5-fold CV on each
true function  k-NN MSE  tree MSE  tree - kNN (mean)     SE  mean k  mean leaves
         step    0.0226    0.0101            -0.0126 0.0023 10.3000       2.2000
         sine    0.0175    0.0408             0.0233 0.0014  7.6500       7.8000

On the step the tree is far better: its mean squared error is 0.0101 against 0.0226 for kkk-NN, and the difference of -0.0126 is more than five standard errors (0.0023). Cross-validation chooses on average 2.2 leaves for the tree (the true function has two pieces) and k≈10k\approx10k≈10 for kkk-NN, a compromise that smooths the jump (Figure 11.5(a), where the kkk-NN curve rounds the corner and wobbles on the flat parts while the tree has one split). On the smooth function the order is reversed: the tree has an error of 0.0408 against 0.0175, a difference of +0.0233 (more than ten standard errors), because a staircase with about 8 steps approximates a sine less well than a local average of 7 neighbors (Figure 11.5(b)). This is the inductive bias of Chapter 3 in its simplest form: piecewise constant is the right assumption for the first function and the wrong one for the second, and no method is better for both. (Smoothing the staircase is one of the things that averaging many trees does, Section 11.6.)

11.5.3 Irrelevant features¶

Section 4.7.2 appended columns of Gaussian noise to the Breast Cancer features and measured how the accuracy of kkk-NN collapses, and Chapter 10 how the lasso copes. A tree handles irrelevant features in a different way: a feature is used only if it gives the best split at some node, and a noise column has a good chance of doing so only where few examples remain. The next cell repeats the experiment of Section 4.7.2 (15 random stratified splits of the whole data set, m=0m=0m=0, 100 and 1000 added noise columns) for a single tree, 5-NN and logistic regression, both standardized.

def noise_experiment(models, ms=(0, 100, 1000), reps=15):
    """Mean test accuracy over random stratified 75/25 splits of the whole Breast Cancer data, with m appended noise columns."""
    out = {name: {m: [] for m in ms} for name in models}
    for r in range(reps):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(r)
        noise = rng.standard_normal((bc.data.shape[0], max(ms)))
        for m in ms:
            X = np.hstack([bc.data, noise[:, :m]])
            a, b, c, d = train_test_split(X, bc_y_all, test_size=0.25, random_state=r, stratify=bc_y_all)
            for name, make in models.items():
                out[name][m].append(make().fit(a, c).score(b, d))
    return out


models_noise = {"tree": lambda: DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=SEED),
                "5-NN": lambda: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(5)),
                "logistic": lambda: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=1, max_iter=3000))}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
noise_res = noise_experiment(models_noise)
print(pd.DataFrame({name: {f"m = {m}": np.mean(v) for m, v in res.items()} for name, res in noise_res.items()}).to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))
print(f"(15 splits; standard error of each mean about {np.mean([np.std(v, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(15) for res in noise_res.values() for v in res.values()]):.3f})")
print(f"[{time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s]")
          tree  5-NN  logistic
m = 0    0.925 0.961     0.974
m = 100  0.912 0.902     0.945
m = 1000 0.906 0.819     0.915
(15 splits; standard error of each mean about 0.005)
[2.1 s]

Without noise columns the tree is the weakest of the three (0.925, against 0.961 for 5-NN and 0.974 for the logistic regression). With 1000 noise columns the tree has lost 0.019 of accuracy, the logistic regression 0.059 and 5-NN 0.142, and the order of 5-NN and the tree is reversed: 0.906 against 0.819 (the standard error of each mean is about 0.005). This is the observation of Section 4.7.2 turned into a method: a tree chooses where to look, so a thousand irrelevant columns are a thousand extra candidates for each split but do not enter the distances. The comparison is also a caution: the tree is not the best of the three at any mmm. On Breast Cancer the classes are almost linearly separable in a few correlated features, which is exactly the case for which linear models are built (and Chapter 10 showed that a sparse linear model deals with the noise columns as well).

11.5.4 Axis-aligned boundaries¶

The price of the threshold rules is that every boundary of a tree is made of pieces parallel to the axes. A boundary that is not parallel to an axis must be approximated by a staircase with as many steps as the accuracy requires, while a linear model represents it with one weight vector. The effect is easy to isolate on a constructed problem with a diagonal boundary: x∼U[−1,1]2\mathbf{x}\sim\mathrm{U}[-1,1]^2x∼U[−1,1]2, y=I[x1+x2>0]y=\mathbb{I}[x_1+x_2>0]y=I[x1​+x2​>0], with 5%5\%5% of the labels flipped, n=200n=200n=200 training and 20,00020{,}00020,000 test points; and the same problem rotated by 45∘45^\circ45∘, in which the boundary is x1′=0x_1'=0x1′​=0. On real data the effect depends on how the signal lies relative to the axes: the last lines of the cell rotate the plane of the two best Breast Cancer features and measure the cross-validated accuracy on the training set.

def oblique_data(n, rng, rotate=False):
    X = rng.uniform(-1, 1, (n, 2))
    y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
    flip = rng.random(n) < 0.05
    y = np.where(flip, 1 - y, y)
    if rotate:                                   # rotate the plane by 45 degrees: the boundary becomes x_1' = 0
        c = np.cos(np.pi / 4)
        X = X @ np.array([[c, -c], [c, c]])
    return X, y


rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
res_obl = {}
for rotate in [False, True]:
    Xo, yo = oblique_data(200, rng, rotate)
    Xo_te, yo_te = oblique_data(20000, rng, rotate)
    accs = {f"tree, depth {d}": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=SEED).fit(Xo, yo).score(Xo_te, yo_te) for d in [1, 2, 4, 8]}
    accs["tree, pruned by CV"] = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=SEED), {"ccp_alpha": np.linspace(0, 0.03, 16)}, cv=5).fit(Xo, yo).score(Xo_te, yo_te)
    accs["logistic regression"] = LogisticRegression().fit(Xo, yo).score(Xo_te, yo_te)
    res_obl[rotate] = accs
print("test accuracy on 20,000 constructed points (the Bayes rate is 0.95 for both)")
print(pd.DataFrame({"diagonal boundary": res_obl[False], "boundary parallel to an axis": res_obl[True]}).to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))

# the same experiment on two real features
two = [bc_names.index("worst perimeter"), bc_names.index("worst concave points")]
Z2 = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xb_tr[:, two])
rcv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
rows = []
for theta in [0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90]:
    c, s = np.cos(np.radians(theta)), np.sin(np.radians(theta))
    Zr = Z2 @ np.array([[c, -s], [s, c]])
    rows.append({"rotation (degrees)": theta,
                 "tree, 8 leaves": cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_leaf_nodes=8, random_state=SEED), Zr, yb_tr, cv=rcv).mean(),
                 "logistic": cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), Zr, yb_tr, cv=rcv).mean()})
print("\nBreast Cancer, the plane of worst perimeter and worst concave points rotated; 5-fold CV accuracy on the training set")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))

On the diagonal boundary the tree needs depth to approximate the line and still does not reach it: its accuracy is 0.706 for a single split, 0.804 with two, 0.885 with four, and falls to 0.828 with eight levels, where the staircase starts to follow the flipped labels; the tree pruned by cross-validation reaches 0.881. The logistic regression, which represents the boundary exactly, reaches 0.933 (the Bayes rate of 0.95 is the ceiling). When the same problem is rotated by 45∘45^\circ45∘ the boundary is x1′=0x_1'=0x1′​=0, a single split suffices (0.948 at depth 1), and the tree and the logistic regression (0.946) are equal. The bias is therefore a statement about the coordinates: a tree is good when the signal is aligned with the features. On the real data the effect is not visible: for the plane of two Breast Cancer features the tree is between 0.925 and 0.948 at all angles, with no pattern, while the logistic regression, which is invariant to rotations, has 0.937 throughout; differences of 0.02 are of the order of the binomial standard error of an accuracy near 0.93 on 426 patients (0.012). The staircase of Figure 11.6(b) is the price, and it is paid only when the true boundary is oblique, which is common in problems where the features are sums or ratios of the quantities that matter (one can add such combinations, or rotate the features by a PCA, as Chapter 13 will teach).

11.5.5 Instability¶

The last property is the one that motivates the rest of the chapter. The root split of the Breast Cancer tree was the worst perimeter at 112.8, with two runners-up almost as good (Section 11.3.2), and the split of Diabetes at depth 4 was a coin toss between equal gains (Section 11.2.2). If the best split is a near-tie, a small change of the data changes it, and everything below it. The cell draws 200 bootstrap samples of the training set (nnn examples drawn with replacement, as in the bootstrap of Section 6.2.4), grows a depth-one tree on each, and counts the feature of the root split; and it measures how often two full trees grown on different bootstrap samples classify a test patient differently.

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
n_tr = len(yb_tr)
root_counts, boot_trees = {}, []
for b in range(200):
    idx = rng.integers(0, n_tr, n_tr)
    stump = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=SEED).fit(Xb_tr[idx], yb_tr[idx])
    name = bc_names[stump.tree_.feature[0]]
    root_counts[name] = root_counts.get(name, 0) + 1
    if b < 40:
        boot_trees.append(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=SEED).fit(Xb_tr[idx], yb_tr[idx]))
root_tab = pd.Series(root_counts).sort_values(ascending=False)
print("feature of the root split over 200 bootstrap samples of the training set:")
print(root_tab.to_string())

preds = np.array([t.predict(Xb_te) for t in boot_trees])                  # 40 full trees on the 143 test patients
pairs = [(i, j) for i in range(40) for j in range(i + 1, 40)]
disagree = np.mean([np.mean(preds[i] != preds[j]) for i, j in pairs])
unstable = np.mean(preds.min(axis=0) != preds.max(axis=0))
print(f"\nTwo full trees grown on different bootstrap samples disagree on {disagree:.1%} of the test patients on average;")
print(f"among the 40 trees, {unstable:.1%} of the test patients receive different predictions from different trees")
acc_trees = np.array([np.mean(p == yb_te) for p in preds])
print(f"test accuracy of the 40 trees: mean {acc_trees.mean():.3f}, standard deviation {acc_trees.std(ddof=1):.3f}, range {acc_trees.min():.3f} to {acc_trees.max():.3f}")

The root split is the worst perimeter in 115 of the 200 samples (57.5%57.5\%57.5%), but 85 samples choose another feature, five different ones in all (Figure 11.7(a)): the near-ties of Section 11.3.2 are real. Two full trees grown on different bootstrap samples disagree on 9.7%9.7\%9.7% of the test patients on average, and among 40 such trees 39.2%39.2\%39.2% of the test patients receive different predictions from different trees. The test accuracy of the 40 trees averages 0.919, with a standard deviation of 0.021 and a range from 0.874 to 0.965: the same algorithm on slightly different data gives models whose accuracies differ by about nine points, which is the high variance of a 1-NN-like model. On the one-feature Diabetes problem (Figure 11.7(b)) the 25 bootstrap trees of depth 4 are all staircases, each with its own steps, and their average, the thick curve, is a much smoother function that follows the trend of the data. Averaging a high-variance, low-bias predictor reduces the variance and keeps the bias; the next section makes this precise.

def figure_11_5():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.2))
    for ax, (name, f) in zip(axes, worlds.items()):

11.5.6 Summary of the inductive bias¶

A tree (i) is invariant to monotone transformations of each feature; (ii) averages over neighborhoods that it chooses from the targets, narrow where the function jumps and wide where it is flat, which is excellent for piecewise-constant signals and poor for smooth ones; (iii) deals with irrelevant features better than distance-based methods but not better than a sparse linear model when the truth is linear; (iv) draws axis-aligned boundaries, which is a cost for oblique ones; and (v) has high variance, because its greedy choices are unstable. The first four are the strengths and weaknesses of the model class; the fifth is a property of the algorithm, and it can be removed without touching the others. That is the programme of the rest of the chapter.

11.6 Bagging and random forests¶

11.6.1 The variance of an average¶

Section 11.5.5 ended with the suggestion that averaging many trees removes most of the variance. How much can it remove? Let Z1,…,ZBZ_1,\dots,Z_BZ1​,…,ZB​ be the predictions at a fixed point x\mathbf{x}x of BBB trees. They have the same distribution (the trees are grown by the same randomized procedure), but they are not independent, because they are all grown on the same training set.

Proposition 11.8 (variance of an average of correlated predictors)

Let Z1,…,ZBZ_1,\dots,Z_BZ1​,…,ZB​ have the same mean μ\muμ, the same variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 and pairwise correlation ρ\rhoρ. Then the average Zˉ=1B∑bZb\bar Z=\frac1B\sum_bZ_bZˉ=B1​∑b​Zb​ has mean μ\muμ and

Var⁡(Zˉ)=ρ σ2+1−ρB σ2.(11.2)\operatorname{Var}(\bar Z)=\rho\,\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\,\sigma^2 . \tag{11.2}Var(Zˉ)=ρσ2+B1−ρ​σ2.(11.2)
(7)

Proof. Var⁡(∑bZb)=∑bVar⁡(Zb)+∑b≠b′Cov⁡(Zb,Zb′)=Bσ2+B(B−1)ρσ2\operatorname{Var}(\sum_bZ_b)=\sum_b\operatorname{Var}(Z_b)+\sum_{b\neq b'}\operatorname{Cov}(Z_b,Z_{b'})=B\sigma^2+B(B-1)\rho\sigma^2Var(∑b​Zb​)=∑b​Var(Zb​)+∑b=b′​Cov(Zb​,Zb′​)=Bσ2+B(B−1)ρσ2, and dividing by B2B^2B2 gives σ2/B+(1−1/B)ρσ2=ρσ2+(1−ρ)σ2/B\sigma^2/B+(1-1/B)\rho\sigma^2=\rho\sigma^2+(1-\rho)\sigma^2/Bσ2/B+(1−1/B)ρσ2=ρσ2+(1−ρ)σ2/B. The mean of an average is the common mean. ■\blacksquare■

Two consequences organize the section. The bias is not reduced: the average has the expectation of a single tree, so averaging helps only a predictor that has a low bias and a high variance, and a full-depth tree is exactly that. The variance cannot go below ρσ2\rho\sigma^2ρσ2: with independent predictors (ρ=0\rho=0ρ=0) it would vanish as 1/B1/B1/B, but correlated ones stop improving at ρσ2\rho\sigma^2ρσ2, however many we average. To gain more, one must reduce ρ\rhoρ, by making the trees different from one another, even at the price of a larger σ2\sigma^2σ2 for each. Here “the variance” is over the randomness of both the training sample and the algorithm; the experiment of Section 11.6.4 measures ρ\rhoρ and σ2\sigma^2σ2 in that sense.

11.6.2 Bagging¶

Bagging (bootstrap aggregating; Breiman, 1996) produces different trees from the one training set by growing each on a bootstrap sample: nnn examples drawn with replacement. The prediction is the average of the BBB trees (regression), or the average of their class probabilities or the majority vote (classification). The bootstrap sample is a cheap way to ask “what would the tree have been with slightly different data?”, and the average is the answer to that question, as seen in Figure 11.7(b).

Proposition 11.9 (what a bootstrap sample contains)

Each training example is missing from a bootstrap sample of size nnn with probability (1−1/n)n→e−1≈0.368(1-1/n)^n\to e^{-1}\approx0.368(1−1/n)n→e−1≈0.368. A bootstrap sample therefore contains on average n(1−(1−1/n)n)≈0.632 nn\big(1-(1-1/n)^n\big)\approx0.632\,nn(1−(1−1/n)n)≈0.632n distinct examples, and each example is out of the bag for about 36.8%36.8\%36.8% of the trees.

Proof. Each of the nnn draws misses a given example with probability 1−1/n1-1/n1−1/n, independently, and (1−1/n)n→e−1(1-1/n)^n\to e^{-1}(1−1/n)n→e−1. The expected number of distinct examples is the sum of the inclusion probabilities. ■\blacksquare■

This gives bagging an error estimate for free. For each example iii, average only the trees for which iii was out of the bag (the OOB prediction): the trees have not seen iii, so the prediction is an honest one, and the average of the losses over iii is the out-of-bag error. It resembles leave-one-out cross-validation (Section 5.3), with the caveat that each OOB prediction uses only about 0.368B0.368B0.368B trees, each grown on about 0.632n0.632n0.632n distinct examples, so it is slightly pessimistic for a forest of BBB trees grown on nnn examples. No separate validation set and no refits are needed, which makes it a convenient tool for tuning forests (Section 11.6.5). The next cell checks the proposition on the 331 Diabetes patients.

n_d = len(yd_tr)
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
distinct_frac, oob_share = [], np.zeros(n_d)
for b in range(2000):
    idx = rng.integers(0, n_d, n_d)
    distinct_frac.append(len(np.unique(idx)) / n_d)
    oob_share += ~np.isin(np.arange(n_d), idx)
print(f"(1 - 1/n)^n for n = {n_d}: {(1 - 1 / n_d) ** n_d:.4f};  limit exp(-1) = {np.exp(-1):.4f}")
print(f"2000 bootstrap samples: distinct examples {np.mean(distinct_frac):.4f} of n (predicted {1 - (1 - 1 / n_d) ** n_d:.4f});"
      f" each example is out of the bag in {np.mean(oob_share / 2000):.4f} of the samples on average"
      f" (smallest {np.min(oob_share / 2000):.3f}, largest {np.max(oob_share / 2000):.3f})")
(1 - 1/n)^n for n = 331: 0.3673;  limit exp(-1) = 0.3679
2000 bootstrap samples: distinct examples 0.6326 of n (predicted 0.6327); each example is out of the bag in 0.3674 of the samples on average (smallest 0.341, largest 0.395)

The simulation agrees with the proposition: (1−1/n)n=0.3673(1-1/n)^n=0.3673(1−1/n)n=0.3673 for n=331n=331n=331, against the limit e−1=0.3679e^{-1}=0.3679e−1=0.3679; in 2000 bootstrap samples of the Diabetes training set the average number of distinct examples is 0.6326 n0.6326\,n0.6326n (the formula gives 0.6327 n0.6327\,n0.6327n), and an example is out of the bag in 36.74%36.74\%36.74% of the samples on average. Across the 331 examples the proportion runs from 34.1%34.1\%34.1% to 39.5%39.5\%39.5%, which is the spread that 2000 samples produce (the standard error of a proportion near 0.37 is 0.011).

The out-of-bag examples are a free validation set. The OOB prediction of the example iii is the average of the trees that did not see it, and the OOB error is the error of these predictions. Each OOB prediction averages about a third of the forest, so it behaves like the prediction of a smaller forest and is slightly pessimistic, but it costs no extra fitting and uses no data held back: it is a form of cross-validation that comes with the training.

11.6.3 Random forests¶

Bagging reduces the variance but leaves a correlation ρ\rhoρ between the trees: they are all grown on resamples of the same data, and the same strong features win the same splits, so that all the trees start with the same few splits. A random forest (Breiman, 2001) lowers ρ\rhoρ by an extra randomization: at each split only a random subset of mtrym_{\text{try}}mtry​ of the ppp features is considered, and the best split among those is used. The default is mtry=pm_{\text{try}}=\sqrt pmtry​=p​ for classification and p/3p/3p/3 for regression; mtry=pm_{\text{try}}=pmtry​=p is bagging. Each tree is a little worse than a bagged tree, because it is denied the best split at some nodes (its variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 is larger and its bias is also larger), but the trees are much less alike, and by (11.2) the average gains more than the individual loses, if ρ\rhoρ falls enough. The trees are grown to full depth (or until min_samples_leaf examples remain), without pruning: the averaging, not the pruning, controls the variance.

Algorithm (random forest)

For b=1,…,Bb=1,\dots,Bb=1,…,B: draw a bootstrap sample of the training set; grow a tree on it, and at every node consider only mtrym_{\text{try}}mtry​ features chosen at random for that node, choosing the best split among them; do not prune. The prediction is the average of the trees (regression) or of their class probabilities (classification).

11.6.4 Measuring ρ\rhoρ and σ2\sigma^2σ2¶

Proposition 11.8 is a statement about the correlation between trees over both the training sample and the randomization. To measure it we need many training sets, which a real data set does not provide. We use the 331 Diabetes training patients as a population from which we draw R=100R=100R=100 training sets of n=100n=100n=100 patients without replacement (a resampling experiment, in the spirit of Chapter 6’s simulation on a real design); for each we grow a forest of 100 trees, either bagging (mtry=pm_{\text{try}}=pmtry​=p) or a random forest with mtry=p/3m_{\text{try}}=p/3mtry​=p/3, and record the predictions of every tree at the 111 test points. Then, at each point, σ2\sigma^2σ2 is the variance over the data sets of one tree’s prediction, ρσ2\rho\sigma^2ρσ2 is the covariance of two different trees of the same forest (estimated on disjoint pairs, so that it does not use the variance of the averages), and the variance of the average of BBB trees is measured directly from the first BBB trees. Equation (11.2) can then be tested: it predicts the variance of the average from σ2\sigma^2σ2 and ρσ2\rho\sigma^2ρσ2 alone.

def variance_study(max_features, R=100, n=100, B_max=100, Bs=(1, 5, 20, 100)):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    preds = np.empty((R, B_max, len(yd_te)))
    for r in range(R):
        idx = rng.choice(len(yd_tr), n, replace=False)
        forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=B_max, max_features=max_features, random_state=r).fit(Xd_tr[idx], yd_tr[idx])
        preds[r] = np.array([t.predict(Xd_te) for t in forest.estimators_])
    sigma2 = preds.var(axis=0, ddof=1).mean(axis=0)                         # (m,)  variance of one tree over the data sets, per test point
    centered = preds - preds.mean(axis=0)
    cov_pairs = np.mean([(centered[:, 2 * i] * centered[:, 2 * i + 1]).sum(axis=0) / (R - 1) for i in range(B_max // 2)], axis=0)   # covariance of two trees
    rows = []
    for B in Bs:
        measured = preds[:, :B].mean(axis=1).var(axis=0, ddof=1).mean()
        predicted = np.mean(cov_pairs + (sigma2 - cov_pairs) / B)           # equation (11.2) at each point, averaged over the points
        rows.append({"B": B, "measured variance of the average": measured, "equation (11.2)": predicted})
    rho = cov_pairs.mean() / sigma2.mean()
    return pd.DataFrame(rows), sigma2.mean(), rho, preds


t0 = time.perf_counter()
var_tabs, var_info = {}, {}
for name, mf in [("bagging (m_try = p)", 1.0), ("random forest (m_try = p/3)", 1 / 3)]:
    tab, s2, rho, _ = variance_study(mf)
    var_tabs[name], var_info[name] = tab, (s2, rho)
    print(f"{name}:  sigma^2 = {s2:.0f}   rho = {rho:.3f}   rho sigma^2 = {rho * s2:.0f}")
    print(tab.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.0f}"))
print(f"[{time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s]")
