  • Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic): W. N. Street, W. H. Wolberg and O. L. Mangasarian, “Nuclear feature extraction for breast tumor diagnosis”, IS&T/SPIE 1993 International Symposium on Electronic Imaging: Science and Technology, volume 1905, 861–870 (1993). Bundled with scikit-learn. Malignant =1=1=1; the stratified 426/143 split of Chapters 6 to 10.

  • Digits: E. Alpaydin and C. Kaynak, “Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits”, UCI Machine Learning Repository (1998). Bundled with scikit-learn; all ten classes, the stratified 1347/4501347/4501347/450 split of Chapters 6 and 9 (Section 11.11).

  • Wine: M. Forina et al., “PARVUS: An Extendible Package for Data Exploration, Classification and Correlation”, Institute of Pharmaceutical and Food Analysis and Technologies, Genoa (1991), UCI Machine Learning Repository. Bundled with scikit-learn (Exercise 11.6).

  • Constructed and simulated data (flagged in the text): the six-point worked example of Section 11.2.3; the step and sine functions with Gaussian noise of Section 11.5.2; the noise columns appended to real features (Sections 11.5.3, 11.6.7, 11.7 and Exercises 11.10); the diagonal boundary with flipped labels of Section 11.5.4; the resampling experiment of Section 11.6.4, which draws training sets from the real Diabetes patients; the shuffled-label noise problem of Section 11.7.3; and the small numerical examples of Exercises 11.1 to 11.5.

Further reading¶

  • L. Breiman, J. H. Friedman, R. A. Olshen and C. J. Stone, Classification and Regression Trees, Wadsworth, 1984. The origin of trees as used here: greedy splitting, impurities, cost-complexity pruning (Section 11.4) and cross-validated choice of the subtree.

  • J. R. Quinlan, “Induction of decision trees”, Machine Learning 1(1), 81–106 (1986), and C4.5: Programs for Machine Learning, Morgan Kaufmann, 1993. The entropy-based line of algorithms, developed in parallel in machine learning.

  • L. Breiman, “Bagging predictors”, Machine Learning 24(2), 123–140 (1996), and “Random forests”, Machine Learning 45(1), 5–32 (2001). Bagging, random forests, the out-of-bag error and the permutation importance (Sections 11.6 and 11.7).

  • T. G. Dietterich, “An experimental comparison of three methods for constructing ensembles of decision trees: bagging, boosting, and randomization”, Machine Learning 40(2), 139–157 (2000), and P. Geurts, D. Ernst and L. Wehenkel, “Extremely randomized trees”, Machine Learning 63(1), 3–42 (2006) (Exercise 11.8).

  • Y. Freund and R. E. Schapire, “A decision-theoretic generalization of on-line learning and an application to boosting”, Journal of Computer and System Sciences 55(1), 119–139 (1997). AdaBoost and the bound of Theorem 11.12.

  • R. E. Schapire, Y. Freund, P. Bartlett and W. S. Lee, “Boosting the margin: a new explanation for the effectiveness of voting methods”, Annals of Statistics 26(5), 1651–1686 (1998), and L. Breiman, “Prediction games and arcing algorithms”, Neural Computation 11(7), 1493–1517 (1999). The margin explanation and the objections to it, with the behavior seen in Section 11.8.3. R. E. Schapire and Y. Freund, Boosting: Foundations and Algorithms, MIT Press, 2012, for the whole theory.

  • J. Friedman, T. Hastie and R. Tibshirani, “Additive logistic regression: a statistical view of boosting”, Annals of Statistics 28(2), 337–407 (2000). AdaBoost as stagewise minimization of the exponential loss, the log-odds it estimates and the Gentle AdaBoost of Exercise 11.5.

  • J. H. Friedman, “Greedy function approximation: a gradient boosting machine”, Annals of Statistics 29(5), 1189–1232 (2001), and “Stochastic gradient boosting”, Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 38(4), 367–378 (2002). Sections 11.9.1 and 11.9.4.

  • T. Chen and C. Guestrin, “XGBoost: a scalable tree boosting system”, Proceedings of KDD 2016, 785–794, and G. Ke et al., “LightGBM: a highly efficient gradient boosting decision tree”, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (2017). The regularized second-order objective of Proposition 11.14 and the histogram algorithms.

  • A. Niculescu-Mizil and R. Caruana, “Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning”, Proceedings of ICML 2005, 625–632. The calibration of forests, boosting and other classifiers (Section 11.10).

  • C. Strobl, A.-L. Boulesteix, A. Zeileis and T. Hothorn, “Bias in random forest variable importance measures: illustrations, sources and a solution”, BMC Bioinformatics 8, 25 (2007). The bias of the impurity importance toward columns with many distinct values (Section 11.7.1).

  • L. Grinsztajn, E. Oyallon and G. Varoquaux, “Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data?”, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35, Datasets and Benchmarks Track (2022). A benchmark on tabular data (Section 11.11).

  • T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani and J. Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd edition, Springer, 2009 (free online), Chapters 9, 10, 15 and 16. The standard reference for the whole chapter.

11.13 Exercises¶

Difficulty: ★ warm-up, ★★ core, ★★★ challenge. Try each exercise before reading the hint; solutions and detailed outlines are in Appendix C.

Manual (analytical) exercises¶

Exercise 11.1 ★ — A tree and its pruning by hand. (Constructed numbers.) One feature and eight points: x=(1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8)x=(1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8)x=(1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8) and y=(3,1,2,9,11,10,4,5)y=(3,1,2,9,11,10,4,5)y=(3,1,2,9,11,10,4,5). (a) Find the first split of a regression tree and its gain by Proposition 11.2, and check it against the residual sums of squares. (b) Grow the tree greedily to depth 2 (a split in each child of the root, with the best threshold in each) and write its four leaf values and its training RSS. (c) For this tree compute g(t)g(t)g(t) for each internal node, prune the weakest link, recompute the values of ggg for the pruned tree and continue until only the root is left: list the nested subtrees and the values of α\alphaα at which they change.

Hint. The gain of a threshold is nLnRn(yˉL−yˉR)2\frac{n_Ln_R}{n}(\bar y_L-\bar y_R)^2nnL​nR​​(yˉ​L​−yˉ​R​)2. The criterion is g(t)=(R(t)−R(Tt))/(∣Tt∣−1)g(t)=\big(R(t)-R(T_t)\big)/(\lvert T_t\rvert-1)g(t)=(R(t)−R(Tt​))/(∣Tt​∣−1), with R(t)R(t)R(t) the RSS of the node taken as a leaf and R(Tt)R(T_t)R(Tt​) the total RSS of the leaves of its subtree. The values of ggg change after a pruning, because the subtrees change.

Exercise 11.2 ★★ — The Gini gain in closed form. For two classes with proportion ppp of class 1 in a node, the Gini index is 2p(1−p)2p(1-p)2p(1−p). (a) Show that a split of a node of nnn examples into children of sizes nL,nRn_L,n_RnL​,nR​ and proportions pL,pRp_L,p_RpL​,pR​ has Gini gain 2 nLnRn2(pL−pR)22\,\frac{n_Ln_R}{n^2}(p_L-p_R)^22n2nL​nR​​(pL​−pR​)2. (b) Compute it for a node with 50 examples of class 0 and 10 of class 1 that is split into (25,0)(25,0)(25,0) and (25,10)(25,10)(25,10). (c) For the same split compute the gain in misclassification rate; why does a tree grown with the misclassification rate have trouble choosing it, and what does Proposition 11.4 say about the Gini index here?

Hint. (a) The weighted average of pLp_LpL​ and pRp_RpR​ is ppp, so p(1−p)=p−p2p(1-p)=p-p^2p(1−p)=p−p2 and the gain is 2[nLnpL2+nRnpR2−p2]2\big[\frac{n_L}{n}p_L^2+\frac{n_R}{n}p_R^2-p^2\big]2[nnL​​pL2​+nnR​​pR2​−p2], a variance. (c) Compare the errors of the parent and of the children when the majority class does not change.

Python (computational) exercises¶

Exercise 11.6 ★ — Pruning on Wine. Use the Wine data (load_wine, three classes, 13 features), a stratified 75%/25%75\%/25\%75%/25% split (random_state=SEED). (a) Grow the full tree and compute its cost-complexity path (cost_complexity_pruning_path); plot the number of leaves against α\alphaα. (b) Choose α\alphaα by 10-fold stratified cross-validation at the minimum of the error and by the one-SE rule, and report the number of leaves of each. (c) On the test set compare the full tree, the two pruned trees, a random forest of 300 trees, AdaBoost with stumps (use AdaBoostClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1)) with the number of rounds chosen by cross-validation) and a standardized logistic regression: errors and binomial standard errors. What can and cannot be concluded?

Hint. The path’s ccp_alphas have a last value that leaves only the root; evaluate cross-validation at the distinct values, as in Section 11.4.3. The standard error of an error rate e^\hat ee^ on nnn test examples is e^(1−e^)/n\sqrt{\hat e(1-\hat e)/n}e^(1−e^)/n​.

Exercise 11.7 ★★ — A forest from scratch and its OOB error. On the Diabetes training set, implement a random forest regressor with B=300B=300B=300 trees: a bootstrap sample for each tree and DecisionTreeRegressor(max_features=1/3, min_samples_leaf=5); keep for each patient the list of trees for which it is out of the bag. (a) Compute the OOB prediction of every patient and the OOB RMSE, and compare with RandomForestRegressor(..., oob_score=True) with the same parameters, and the test RMSE of both. (b) For B=10B=10B=10 trees, how many training patients are in the bootstrap sample of every tree, and hence have no OOB prediction? Compare with the expected number n (1−e−1)Bn\,(1-e^{-1})^Bn(1−e−1)B (approximately) and with a simulation.

Hint. rng.integers(0, n, n) draws a bootstrap sample; a patient is out of the bag for tree bbb if it does not appear in it. The probability that a patient appears in a given bootstrap sample is about 0.632.

Exercise 11.8 ★★ — Extremely randomized trees. Repeat the resampling experiment of Section 11.6.4 (training sets of n=100n=100n=100 patients drawn without replacement from the 331 Diabetes training patients, predictions at the 111 test points) with R=40R=40R=40 training sets and B=50B=50B=50 trees, for RandomForestRegressor and for ExtraTreesRegressor (random thresholds, no bootstrap), both with max_features=1/3 and min_samples_leaf=5. Estimate σ2\sigma^2σ2, ρ\rhoρ and the variance of the average of the 50 trees for each; also compute the test RMSE of both forests grown on the whole training set. Where does the extra randomization of the extremely randomized trees act, on σ2\sigma^2σ2 or on ρ\rhoρ, and what does it cost?

Hint. For each data set, collect the predictions of the BBB trees ([t.predict(X_test) for t in forest.estimators_]); σ2\sigma^2σ2 is the variance over data sets of one tree’s prediction, averaged over trees and test points, and ρσ2\rho\sigma^2ρσ2 is the covariance of two different trees, estimated on disjoint pairs.

Exercise 11.9 ★★★ — Newton boosting for the logistic loss. On Breast Cancer implement gradient boosting with the logistic loss and F0=ln⁡yˉ1−yˉF_0=\ln\frac{\bar y}{1-\bar y}F0​=ln1−yˉ​yˉ​​: at each round fit a DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2) to the pseudo-residuals yi−piy_i-p_iyi​−pi​, then replace each leaf value by the Newton value ∑i∈Rj(yi−pi)/∑i∈Rjpi(1−pi)\sum_{i\in R_j}(y_i-p_i)\big/\sum_{i\in R_j}p_i(1-p_i)∑i∈Rj​​(yi​−pi​)/∑i∈Rj​​pi​(1−pi​) (equation (11.4) with λ=0\lambda=0λ=0), and update F←F+νfF\leftarrow F+\nu fF←F+νf with ν=0.1\nu=0.1ν=0.1. (a) Compare the decision function after 20 and 100 rounds with that of GradientBoostingClassifier with the same parameters on the test inputs. (b) Plot the 5-fold cross-validated log loss against the number of rounds up to 300 for your implementation, and report its minimum. (c) Repeat with the leaf value ∑(yi−pi)/(∑pi(1−pi)+λ)\sum(y_i-p_i)/\big(\sum p_i(1-p_i)+\lambda\big)∑(yi​−pi​)/(∑pi​(1−pi​)+λ) for λ=1,10\lambda=1,10λ=1,10: what changes?

Hint. The leaf of a training point is tree.apply(X); accumulate the sums with np.bincount(leaf, weights=...) and give the new value to the tree through tree.tree_.value, or keep the leaf values in a separate array indexed by leaf. Expect an agreement to rounding for the first rounds, and a possible divergence later at exact ties (Section 11.9.2).

Exercise 11.10 ★★★ — Importances of correlated features on Diabetes. Fit a random forest of 300 trees (max_features=1/3, min_samples_leaf=5) on 75%75\%75% of the Diabetes training patients and use the remaining 25%25\%25% for the permutation importance. (a) Compute the MDI and the permutation importance (the increase of the RMSE, 30 permutations) of each of the 10 features, with a bootstrap over the validation patients (500 resamples) for a confidence interval of each permutation importance. (b) Permute together the group s1, s2 (correlation about 0.9, Section 6.2.4) and compare the increase of the RMSE with those of the two features permuted separately. (c) Append 20 Gaussian noise columns (constructed) and report the largest MDI and the largest permutation importance among them. (d) Which features does the lasso of Chapter 10 keep at the one-SE value of λ\lambdaλ? Compare the lists.

Hint. permutation_importance(..., scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error") returns decreases of the score; for the group, copy the columns of a permuted row index as in Section 11.7.2. Store, for every feature and every permutation, the predictions on the validation patients; the bootstrap resamples the patients and recomputes the increase of the RMSE from the stored predictions.

What comes next¶

Everything in Chapters 4 to 11 had the same ingredients: examples xi\mathbf{x}_ixi​ with labels yiy_iyi​, a loss that measures the disagreement between a prediction and a label, and a model class searched for a small loss. A tree divides the space into boxes and puts the mean of the labels in each box (Proposition 11.1); the model selection of Chapter 5 chooses its size; the ensembles of this chapter average or add many trees to cure the variance or the bias that a single tree has. Chapter 12 takes the labels away. With only the examples x1,…,xn\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_nx1​,…,xn​, the question becomes whether they fall into groups, and what a good partition means when no label can say. The answer of clustering has a familiar form: kkk-means chooses the partition and the centers that minimize the within-cluster sum of squares, and for a fixed partition the best center of a cluster is, again, its mean, the statement of Proposition 11.1 with no target. The tree is a supervised partition into boxes, found greedily by the labels; kkk-means is an unsupervised partition into cells around centers, found by alternating two steps that each decrease the same objective. We shall see where the objective is hard (it is NP-hard in general), what the alternation guarantees and does not, how to choose the number of groups when there is no validation error, and why the same data can legitimately be clustered in different ways. We close with the difference between the unsupervised and the semi-supervised settings promised in Chapter 1. Gradient descent, which Section 11.9.1 used in the space of functions, returns in Chapters 14 and 15 in the space of the parameters of a neural network, where the gradients are computed by backpropagation.
